screens.title: The Dynamic Nature of Data
screens.narratorSegment: In the world of data, very little remains static. Information is constantly changing, evolving, and sometimes, becoming obsolete. This dynamic nature means that simply indexing data once isn't enough; we need robust mechanisms to keep it current and relevant. Imagine an e-commerce platform where product prices fluctuate, stock levels change, or descriptions are refined. Or consider a logging system where old log entries need to be purged after a certain retention period. Without efficient ways to update and delete documents, our Elasticsearch index would quickly become stale, inaccurate, and bloated. This not only impacts the quality of search results but also affects storage costs and query performance. Understanding these operations is foundational to building and maintaining a healthy, responsive, and reliable Elasticsearch solution. It's about ensuring your data reflects reality and serves its purpose effectively throughout its lifecycle. The Dynamic Nature of Data means data is rarely static; effective update and delete strategies are vital for maintaining accuracy and performance.. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

screens.title: Full Document Replacement (Re-indexing)
screens.narratorSegment: The simplest way to update a document in Elasticsearch is by performing a full document replacement, often referred to as re-indexing. This method uses the PUT HTTP method, just like when you initially index a document, but you specify an underscore id that already exists in your index. When Elasticsearch receives this request, it doesn't actually modify the existing document in place. Instead, it marks the old document as deleted internally and then indexes the new document you provided. This is why the underscore version number of the document increments with each replacement. A key point to remember is that you must send the *entire* updated document in your request, even if only a single field has changed. For example, if you only want to update a product's price, you still need to include all other fields like name, description, and category in your PUT request. While straightforward, this approach can be less efficient for frequent, small changes, as it involves re-indexing the full document every time. It's best suited for scenarios where most of a document's fields are changing, or when simplicity is prioritized over granular efficiency.

keyIdea.title: PUT for Full Replacement
keyIdea.text: Using PUT with an existing _id replaces the entire document, incrementing its _version.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Full Document Replacement

Full Document Replacement

Replacing an entire document with new data using the PUT method.

# Retrieve product_101 to see its current state and version
curl -X GET "localhost:9200/products/_doc/product_101?pretty"
# Example of a full document replacement (re-index)
# We change the price and description, but must send the entire document again.
curl -X PUT "localhost:9200/products/_doc/product_101?pretty" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d'
{
  "name": "Wireless Ergonomic Mouse",
  "description": "An updated description: A comfortable, high-precision mouse designed for long working hours.",
  "category": "Electronics",
  "sku": "WM-ERGO-001",
  "price": 54.99, # Price updated
  "available": true,
  "created_at": "2023-01-15 10:00:00"
}
'
How it Works

When you `PUT` a document with an existing `_id`, Elasticsearch internally marks the old document as deleted and indexes the new one. This is not an in-place modification.

Version Increment

Each full replacement causes the document's `_version` number to increment, reflecting a new state of the document.

Consideration

You must send the *entire* document, even if only a small part has changed. This can be inefficient for partial updates.

Key Takeaway

Full document replacement is simple but less efficient for minor changes, as it re-indexes the whole document.

screens.title: Targeted Field Updates with `_update` API (Doc)
screens.narratorSegment: For situations where you only need to change a few specific fields within a document, sending the entire document for replacement can be wasteful. This is where Elasticsearch's dedicated underscore update A P I comes in. Unlike the PUT method, the underscore update A P I allows for partial updates, meaning you only send the fields you want to modify. You use a POST request to the underscore update endpoint, specifying the document's underscore id. Inside the request body, you include a doc field, which contains a JSON object with only the fields you wish to update or add. Elasticsearch then fetches the existing document, merges your provided doc object with it, and then re-indexes the modified document. This process is significantly more efficient than fetching the document, modifying it client-side, and then sending the full document back for re-indexing. It reduces network traffic and simplifies client-side logic, making it the preferred method for most partial update scenarios. For example, if a product's price changes, you only need to send the price field within the doc object, not the entire product description and other details.

keyIdea.title: Partial Update Efficiency
keyIdea.text: The _update API with 'doc' allows efficient modification of specific fields, reducing network overhead.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Partial Updates (Doc)

Targeted Field Updates with _update API

Modifying specific fields using the doc approach.

# Partial update using the 'doc' approach
# Only update the 'price' and 'available' fields for product_101
curl -X POST "localhost:9200/products/_update/product_101?pretty" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d'
{
  "doc": {
    "price": 59.99,
    "available": false
  }
}
'
# Expected Response Snippet:
{
  "_index": "products",
  "_id": "product_101",
  "_version": 3, # Version increments
  "result": "updated",
  "_shards": {
    "total": 2,
    "successful": 1,
    "failed": 0
  }
}
How it Works

The `_update` API fetches the existing document, merges the provided `doc` object, and then re-indexes the modified document.

Efficiency Gain

Reduces network payload by only sending changed fields, making it more efficient than full document replacement for minor updates.

Use Case

Ideal for updating a small number of fields, like a product's price or availability status, without touching other data.

Key Takeaway

Use the `_update` API with `doc` for simple, efficient partial updates to specific fields.

screens.title: Dynamic Updates Using Painless Scripts
screens.narratorSegment: Beyond simply merging a doc object, the underscore update A P I offers even greater power through the use of scripts. When your update logic involves calculations, conditional changes, or dynamic field manipulation, a script field within your underscore update request becomes indispensable. Elasticsearch uses a safe and performant scripting language called Painless for these operations. Inside your script, ctx. underscore source provides access to the current document's source fields, allowing you to read, modify, add, or even remove fields programmatically. For instance, you could increment a numeric field by a certain percentage, conditionally set a status based on another field's value, or add a new array element. This approach is incredibly flexible and allows for sophisticated server-side updates without needing to fetch the document, process it client-side, and then send it back. It's particularly useful for atomic operations that need to happen directly on the cluster, ensuring consistency and reducing round trips. Remember, ctx. underscore source is your gateway to the document's data within the script. keyIdea.text: Painless scripts in _update allow complex, dynamic, and conditional modifications directly on the server.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Dynamic Updates (Script)

Dynamic Updates Using Painless Scripts

Performing complex modifications with the script approach.

# Partial update using a 'script'
# Increment the price by 10% for product_101
curl -X POST "localhost:9200/products/_update/product_101?pretty" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d'
{
  "script": {
    "source": "ctx._source.price *= params.factor",
    "lang": "painless",
    "params": {
      "factor": 1.10
    }
  }
}
'
# Expected Response Snippet:
{
  "_index": "products",
  "_id": "product_101",
  "_version": 4, # Version increments again
  "result": "updated",
  "_shards": {
    "total": 2,
    "successful": 1,
    "failed": 0
  }
}
Painless Scripting

Elasticsearch's default scripting language, designed for security and performance, used for complex updates.

`ctx._source` Access

Within a script, `ctx._source` provides direct access to the document's fields, allowing for read and write operations.

Dynamic Logic

Enables calculations, conditional updates, and dynamic addition/removal of fields, all server-side.

Key Takeaway

Use `script` in `_update` for powerful, programmatic, and atomic modifications to your documents.

screens.title: Preventing Lost Updates
screens.narratorSegment: In a system where multiple users or processes might try to update the same document concurrently, there's a risk of 'lost updates.' This happens when one update overwrites another, leading to data inconsistency. Imagine two users simultaneously editing a product description; if one saves their changes just after the other, the first user's update might be completely lost. To prevent this, Elasticsearch implements optimistic concurrency control. This mechanism doesn't lock the document, which could impact performance, but instead relies on versioning. Every document in Elasticsearch has a underscore seq underscore no (sequence number) and a underscore primary underscore term. These values uniquely identify the version of a document. When you retrieve a document, you also get its current underscore seq underscore no and underscore primary underscore term. If you include these values in your subsequent update request, Elasticsearch will only apply your update if these values still match the document's current state. If they don't match, it means another process has modified the document since you last fetched it, and your update will fail with a 409 Conflict error, preventing a lost update. This approach ensures that you are always updating the version of the document you intended to modify.

keyIdea.title: Optimistic Concurrency
keyIdea.text: Using _seq_no and _primary_term prevents lost updates by ensuring you update the expected document version.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Optimistic Concurrency

Preventing Lost Updates

Ensuring data consistency with optimistic concurrency control.

The 'Lost Update' Problem

When multiple processes update the same document, one update can unintentionally overwrite another, leading to data loss.

Optimistic Approach

Instead of locking, Elasticsearch uses versioning (`_seq_no`, `_primary_term`) to ensure updates are applied to the correct document state.

Conflict Resolution

If `_seq_no` or `_primary_term` don't match, the update fails with a `409 Conflict`, preventing accidental overwrites.

Concurrency Control Flow

A visual representation of how optimistic concurrency works.

1. Fetch Document
2. Get `_seq_no`, `_primary_term`
3. Update with `if_seq_no`, `if_primary_term`

screens.title: Concurrency Control in Action
screens.narratorSegment: Let's see how to implement optimistic concurrency control in practice. The first step is to retrieve the document you intend to update. When you perform a GET request, Elasticsearch includes the underscore seq underscore no and underscore primary underscore term in the response metadata. These are the values you'll need to capture. Once you have these, you can include them as parameters in your underscore update request: if underscore seq underscore no and if underscore primary underscore term. For example, if you fetched a document and it had underscore seq underscore no. 5 and underscore primary underscore term. 1, your update request would append? if underscore seq underscore no equals 5&if underscore primary underscore term equals 1 to the endpoint. If, by the time your update request reaches Elasticsearch, another operation has already modified the document, its underscore seq underscore no or underscore primary underscore term will have changed. In this scenario, Elasticsearch will detect the mismatch and respond with a 409 Conflict status code, preventing your update from overwriting the newer changes. This forces your application to handle the conflict, perhaps by re-fetching the document and re-applying the changes, or by notifying the user. This mechanism is crucial for maintaining data integrity in high-concurrency environments, ensuring that every update is based on the most current version of the data.

keyIdea.title: Implementing Concurrency
keyIdea.text: Retrieve _seq_no and _primary_term, then include them in update requests to prevent conflicts.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Concurrency in Action

Concurrency Control in Action

Using if_seq_no and if_primary_term in an update request.

# Example: Retrieve document to get _seq_no and _primary_term
# (Assume product_101 has _seq_no: 5, _primary_term: 1)
curl -X GET "localhost:9200/products/_doc/product_101?pretty"
# Expected GET Response Snippet:
{
  "_index": "products",
  "_id": "product_101",
  "_version": 4,
  "_seq_no": 5, # Capture this value
  "_primary_term": 1, # Capture this value
  "found": true,
  "_source": { ... }
}
# Attempt to update using optimistic concurrency control
# This will only succeed if _seq_no is 5 and _primary_term is 1.
curl -X POST "localhost:9200/products/_update/product_101?if_seq_no=5&if_primary_term=1&pretty" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d'
{
  "doc": {
    "last_updated_by": "admin"
  }
}
'
Retrieve Current State

Always `GET` the document first to obtain its current `_seq_no` and `_primary_term` values.

Include in Update

Pass the retrieved `_seq_no` and `_primary_term` as URL parameters in your `_update` request.

Conflict Response

If the values don't match, Elasticsearch returns a `409 Conflict` error, preventing an outdated update.

Key Takeaway

Optimistic concurrency is a robust way to ensure data integrity in concurrent environments by validating document versions.

screens.title: Deleting Individual Documents
screens.narratorSegment: Just as important as updating documents is the ability to remove them when they are no longer needed. The simplest and most direct way to delete an individual document in Elasticsearch is by using its unique underscore id. This operation is performed using the DELETE HTTP method, targeting the specific document endpoint. For example, to delete a product with underscore id 'product_105' from the 'products' index, you would send a DELETE request to slash products slash underscore doc slash product underscore 105. The response from Elasticsearch will confirm the deletion with result. deleted. It's important to understand that, similar to updates, Elasticsearch doesn't immediately remove the document from disk. Instead, it marks the document as deleted internally. This 'soft delete' mechanism means the document will no longer be returned by search queries, but its space will only be reclaimed during a subsequent segment merge process. This internal behavior is why the underscore version of a deleted document also increments, reflecting its new 'deleted' state. This method is ideal for precise, single-document removals, such as when a specific item is no longer available or a user account is closed.

content.html:
Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › Bulk Deletion

Bulk Deletion with _delete_by_query

Removing multiple documents based on specific criteria.

# Example: Delete all products from the 'Electronics' category that are not available
# IMPORTANT: Always test your query with _search first!
# curl -X GET "localhost:9200/products/_search?pretty" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d'
# {
#   "query": {
#     "bool": {
#       "must": [
#         { "match": { "category.keyword": "Electronics" } },
#         { "match": { "available": false } }
#       ]
#     }
#   }
# }
# '

curl -X POST "localhost:9200/products/_delete_by_query?pretty" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d'
{
  "query": {
    "bool": {
      "must": [
        { "match": { "category.keyword": "Electronics" } },
        { "match": { "available": false } }
      ]
    }
  }
}
'

Deletes all documents that match the specified query criteria, similar to a `DELETE WHERE` clause.

Module 2 › Chapter 2.3 › _delete_by_query Safety

Ensuring Safe _delete_by_query Operations

Essential steps to prevent accidental data loss with bulk deletions.

01

Test Your Query First

Always execute the same query with `_search` to confirm it matches *only* the documents you intend to delete.

02

Use `conflicts=proceed`

Prevents the operation from aborting if version conflicts occur, logging them instead and continuing with other documents.

03

Consider Throttling

For large datasets, use `requests_per_second` to limit the deletion rate and prevent cluster overload.

04

Backup Critical Data

Always consider a snapshot of your cluster before performing large-scale delete operations as a safeguard.

A visual guide to responsible bulk deletion.

2. Execute (`_delete_by_query`)
